title: Turned down at Fredonia, studying saxophone at Potsdam
summary: Rejected at Fredonia for sight singing, he became the first saxophone-only student at Potsdam in 1962 and clashed with Musser and his clarinet teacher.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I see. What were your aspirations? You went to SUNY Potsdam. I had a SUNY experience at Fredonia. And I wonder, when you went there was your jazz interest met at SUNY Potsdam?

I have to say no, but I auditioned for Fredonia first. That’s where I wanted to go because I knew that Don Menza and Sam Noto — or Don Menza had gone there. And there’s a bass player named Linc Milliman who played bass — Linc was basically from six miles outside of Mount Morris is where he grew up, so I used to play with his father, his mother and his sisters and with Linc. And I knew they went to Fredonia so I auditioned for Fredonia but they turned me down because I couldn’t sight sing. You know they made me, like I played, an audition, and then they put a piece of sight singing up there and I never sang anything and so they turned me down. And then I went to Potsdam. See the other thing was that I wasn’t a clarinet player, I was a saxophone player and wanted to get into New York State as a saxophone player. But they didn’t take saxophone players. But the year that I went, in ’62, I was the first saxophone player in the State of New York that was allowed to go into the State of New York school system as just primarily a saxophone player. Because you always had to be a clarinet major and then double on saxophone player for what they had at that time called the “wind ensemble,” you probably remember William Musser had the wind ensemble. So when I went to Potsdam my music — you know at the time he did not want me there. He actually said, “How did you ever get into this school?” You know he was a clarinet major and you know he just © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

did not want me, made it difficult for me. And then there was an opening in the wind ensemble and Joe Roccisano, I don’t know if you know Joe, Joe was a great saxophone player. Joe was going to school at the time and he auditioned me on tenor to go into the wind ensemble, and he said, “Yeah, that’s good. You’ll pass. You can go in.” And my clarinet teacher balked and said, “No I don’t want him in the wind ensemble.” So with that animosity I only lasted one semester. And you know jazz was not — you know the school system at that time, the big band had to rehearse off campus. You couldn’t use the school facilities and all that. But yet they had sent a jazz combo from Potsdam to a Villanova festival and they got all kinds of notification, and a lot of these places got awards. I see Nick Brignola at Ithaca College with Reece Markowitz, they all got noticed and they won this award but yet you couldn’t practice jazz in the practice rooms at Ithaca College. It was a different era back then. Now Potsdam has a great jazz program. All of the schools do. Eastman does — at one time Eastman, you know, forget it.
Well if it’ll make you feel any better regarding Fredonia, Don Menza told me when he was at Fredonia he said practicing bebop was a felony, practicing Dixieland was just a misdemeanor.

Yeah I know Menza told stories about that. It was the turn of a different era of music. And I just happened to be right in the middle of that thing that was turning around in the 60s. And we’re talking 1962. I’m sure about ten years later everything had changed around because every school had to have some kind of big band or jazz band program.
